# Published packages reference

Rimsky publishes on three channels. Go modules carry the code you import, npm carries the wire definitions for JavaScript and TypeScript toolchains, and the GitHub Release carries prebuilt `rimsky` CLI archives. Container images are a fourth channel and are documented separately; this reference names an image only to say where a binary ships.

## What rimsky publishes

| Package | Channel | How to get it | License |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `github.com/rimsky-ai/rimsky-core/lib/protocols` | Go module proxy | `go get github.com/rimsky-ai/rimsky-core/lib/protocols@vX.Y.Z` | Apache-2.0 |
| `github.com/rimsky-ai/rimsky-core` | Git tag `vX.Y.Z` | Not resolvable from outside the repository — see below | AGPL-3.0-or-later, or a Fall Guy Consulting commercial license |
| `@rimsky-ai/protocols` | npm | `npm install @rimsky-ai/protocols` | Apache-2.0 |
| `rimsky_<version>_linux_amd64.tar.gz` | GitHub Release | Download and extract | AGPL-3.0-or-later, or a Fall Guy Consulting commercial license |
| `rimsky_<version>_linux_arm64.tar.gz` | GitHub Release | Download and extract | AGPL-3.0-or-later, or a Fall Guy Consulting commercial license |
| `rimsky_<version>_darwin_amd64.tar.gz` | GitHub Release | Download and extract | AGPL-3.0-or-later, or a Fall Guy Consulting commercial license |
| `rimsky_<version>_darwin_arm64.tar.gz` | GitHub Release | Download and extract | AGPL-3.0-or-later, or a Fall Guy Consulting commercial license |
| `checksums.txt` | GitHub Release | Download beside the archives | — |

The most recent published version is `0.15.0`. The Go module tags, the npm version, and the release archives all carry the same version number for a given release.

## Go modules

Rimsky publishes two Go module paths. Both require Go 1.25.0 or later.

### github.com/rimsky-ai/rimsky-core/lib/protocols

This is the module a consumer depends on. It is the implementer-facing wire contract: everything you link against to speak to rimsky from your own process.

```
go get github.com/rimsky-ai/rimsky-core/lib/protocols@vX.Y.Z
```

The module is self-contained. It requires only third-party packages — `github.com/google/uuid`, `google.golang.org/grpc`, `google.golang.org/protobuf`, and `gopkg.in/yaml.v3` — and imports nothing else from rimsky. Depending on it therefore pulls in no AGPL code.

The generated protobuf and gRPC bindings live at:

```go
import genv1 "github.com/rimsky-ai/rimsky-core/lib/protocols/proto/v1/gen"
```

The module carries the ten `.proto` files, the Go bindings generated from them, protocol server kits, service-authentication enrollment, and the per-protocol conformance libraries the `rimsky conformance` runners drive.

In git, this module's releases are tagged `lib/protocols/vX.Y.Z`. Go maps the subdirectory prefix itself, so you still write `@vX.Y.Z` in the `go get` argument.

### github.com/rimsky-ai/rimsky-core

The root module holds the orchestrator: the scheduler, the supervisor, the control API, the runtime, and the CLI. Every release tags it `vX.Y.Z`.

**A consumer outside this repository cannot fetch it.** The root module requires three sibling modules at version `v0.0.0` and satisfies those requirements with local `replace` directives pointing at directories inside the repository. A consumer's build ignores `replace` directives in a dependency's `go.mod`, and no `v0.0.0` is published for any of the three, so resolution fails. Both of these fail for that reason:

```
go get github.com/rimsky-ai/rimsky-core@vX.Y.Z
go install github.com/rimsky-ai/rimsky-core/cmd/rimsky@vX.Y.Z
```

To run the orchestrator, use a container image. To get the CLI, use a release archive or build from source. To write a service that talks to rimsky, depend on `lib/protocols`.

## npm: @rimsky-ai/protocols

```
npm install @rimsky-ai/protocols
```

The package is Apache-2.0, requires Node 18 or later, and is an ES module. It publishes thirteen files: the ten `.proto` files under `proto/v1`, plus `index.js`, `index.d.ts`, and `package.json`.

It exports exactly two names:

```js
import { protoDir, protoPath } from "@rimsky-ai/protocols";

protoDir;                       // absolute path to the proto/v1 directory
protoPath("executor.proto");    // absolute path to one .proto file
```

A subpath export resolves a `.proto` file directly, for tools that take a specifier rather than a path:

```
@rimsky-ai/protocols/proto/v1/executor.proto
```

**The package ships no generated TypeScript clients.** The name suggests an install-and-import client library, and it is not one. You get the wire definitions and a path to them, and you still run a protobuf toolchain over them yourself. The package is built for `@grpc/proto-loader` and equivalent loaders, which read the `.proto` files at runtime; if you want static TypeScript stubs, generate them in your own build.

The dev channel publishes under the `dev` npm dist-tag:

```
npm install @rimsky-ai/protocols@dev
```

Dev versions take the form `X.Y.Z-dev.YYYYMMDD.gSHA`. The commit SHA is joined into the pre-release segment rather than carried as SemVer build metadata, because `+` is invalid in a Docker tag, is stripped by `npm version`, and is rejected by `go get`.

## GitHub Release archives

The `rimsky` CLI ships as a prebuilt binary, not as a library and not as an image. Each release attaches four archives:

- `rimsky_<version>_linux_amd64.tar.gz`
- `rimsky_<version>_linux_arm64.tar.gz`
- `rimsky_<version>_darwin_amd64.tar.gz`
- `rimsky_<version>_darwin_arm64.tar.gz`

Each archive holds the `rimsky` binary and five license files: `LICENSE.agpl`, `LICENSE.apache`, `NOTICE`, `COPYRIGHT`, and `COPYING.md`. The binaries are built with CGO disabled and carry their version stamped in.

Beside the archives the release attaches `checksums.txt`, covering every archive, and one SBOM per archive named `<archive>.sbom.json`.

There is no Windows archive. The CLI transitively embeds Unix-only process control — process-group creation for spawned daemon processes, and `stat` inode comparison in the filesystem claim producer — so the build matrix is Unix-only by construction.

To install:

1. Download the archive for your platform from the GitHub Release, verify it against `checksums.txt`, and extract the `rimsky` binary onto your `PATH`.
2. Or clone the repository at the release tag and run its `make cli` target, which builds the binary with the version stamped in. A plain `go build` in a checkout also reports the right version, because the binary falls back to its embedded build information when the version stamp is absent.

**The archives cover more platforms than the images do.** Four archives cover both architectures on both operating systems, but the published images are built one architecture at a time, without a multi-platform manifest — at this release every published image carries `linux/arm64` alone. An operator on Apple silicon or Graviton can pull and run; an operator on x86-64 gets a working CLI and no runnable image, and finds out at `docker run`.

## Shipped binaries

Rimsky builds eight binaries.

| Binary | What it does | Where it ships |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rimsky` | The CLI, and more: it also carries the protocol conformance runners, the host daemon, and an in-process rimsky stack that `rimsky run` and `rimsky compose run` self-host when no endpoint resolves | Release archives, and the `rimsky`, `rimsky-all-in-one`, and `rimsky-conformance` images |
| `rimsky-scheduler` | Runs the scheduler role | `rimsky` and `rimsky-all-in-one` images |
| `rimsky-supervisor` | Runs the supervisor role | `rimsky` and `rimsky-all-in-one` images |
| `rimsky-control-api` | Runs the control-API role | `rimsky` and `rimsky-all-in-one` images |
| `rimsky-migrate` | Applies the persistence migrations and exits | `rimsky` and `rimsky-all-in-one` images |
| `rimsky-entrypoint` | PID 1 of the `rimsky` and `rimsky-all-in-one` images; reads the container command and starts the roles | `rimsky` and `rimsky-all-in-one` images |
| `rimsky-host-daemon` | The host daemon as a standalone binary, configured entirely from the environment | No image and no archive — build it from the repository |
| `rimsky-host-daemon-proxy` | The in-stack proxy that host daemons register with and dial through | `rimsky-host-daemon-proxy` image |

Three of these carry a wrinkle worth knowing before you plan a deployment.

**`rimsky-host-daemon` reaches you only as source.** No published image and no release archive contains it. The ordinary route to the host daemon is the CLI: `rimsky daemon start` runs the same daemon out of the `rimsky` binary, re-executing itself in the background and writing its state under the daemon state directory. Build the standalone binary only when you want a daemon supervised by something other than the CLI.

**`rimsky-migrate` is not a role name.** The binary ships inside the `rimsky` image, but the image's entrypoint reads its argument as a role, and `rimsky-migrate` is not one — `docker run … rimsky-migrate` exits 2 with `unknown role "rimsky-migrate"; valid roles: rimsky-scheduler, rimsky-supervisor, rimsky-control-api`. Reach the binary the way a container platform normally names a different command: override the image's entrypoint. Migrations are forward-only; no binary, subcommand, or environment setting runs them down.

**The `rimsky` binary is the whole platform in one file.** Beyond the control-API verbs, it self-hosts a full rimsky stack in-process for one-shot runs, serves the host daemon, and runs the conformance probes. A dev-machine consumer who installs one archive has everything needed to register a template and drive it to terminal without a container.

## Licensing

One line separates the two licenses. The `lib/protocols` module — the wire IDL, the generated bindings, the protocol kits, and the conformance libraries — is Apache-2.0. Everything else rimsky ships, orchestrator and bundled services alike, is AGPL-3.0-or-later or a Fall Guy Consulting commercial license.

The rule that follows: to integrate with rimsky without taking on the AGPL, implement the protocols from your own process against `lib/protocols` or `@rimsky-ai/protocols`, and run rimsky as a separate service. The Apache module imports nothing from the AGPL side, so a dependency on it stays permissive.

Docker Hub's "No AGPL v3 licenses" check reports on an image's third-party supply chain, not on rimsky's own code. A green check there does not mean the image is AGPL-free. Rimsky's binaries are AGPL-3.0-or-later regardless of what that check reports.

## Pre-v1 compatibility

Rimsky is pre-v1. A release may drop a binary, rename a configuration key, or change an environment-variable contract without a deprecation window. Pin a version rather than tracking a floating tag, and read the release notes on every upgrade.
